ranger7.name: Ranger 7
ranger7.young: Ranger 7 was built to crash! It took pictures all the way down, then hit the Moon on purpose.
ranger7.older: Ranger 7 had no landing gear. Its six cameras returned more than 4,300 images in the final minutes before it impacted the Moon on purpose.
ranger7.learned: The first close-up pictures of the Moon taken by a US spacecraft showed that even small areas were covered in craters.
ranger7.now: Broken pieces at the bottom of a small crater it made itself. Its job ended the moment it arrived.

surveyor3.name: Surveyor 3
surveyor3.young: Surveyor 3 landed gently and dug in the dirt with a tiny scoop. Later, astronauts came and visited it!
surveyor3.older: Surveyor 3 bounced twice on landing, then used a scoop to test whether the ground could hold up a heavy spacecraft. Apollo 12 landed within walking distance about two and a half years later.
surveyor3.learned: Lunar soil could support a landing craft. The parts astronauts brought home also showed how metal and cameras age on the Moon.
surveyor3.now: Still standing where it landed, missing its camera and scoop. The camera is on display at the Smithsonian.

apollo11_descent.name: Apollo 11 Descent Stage
apollo11_descent.young: This is the bottom half of the Eagle lander. When the astronauts left, it stayed behind and acted as their launch pad.
apollo11_descent.older: The Lunar Module came in two parts. The descent stage landed the crew on 20 July 1969, then served as the launch platform for the ascent stage that carried them home.
apollo11_descent.learned: It proved people could land on another world and leave again.
apollo11_descent.now: Still on the Moon with a plaque on its leg that reads: 'We came in peace for all mankind.'

lrrr.name: Apollo 11 Laser Reflector
lrrr.young: A panel of 100 special mirrors. Shine a laser at it and the light comes straight back. It needs no power, so it still works!
lrrr.older: Observatories fire laser pulses at its 100 corner-cube prisms and time the return trip, measuring the Earth-Moon distance to within centimeters. It uses no electricity.
lrrr.learned: The Moon is drifting away from Earth by about 3.8 centimeters every year. The data also tests Einstein's theory of gravity.
lrrr.now: Still in use more than 55 years later. Astronauts left it behind, but scientists never stopped using it.

lrv.name: Apollo 15 Lunar Rover
lrv.young: A real electric car on the Moon! Astronauts drove it to explore much farther than they could walk.
lrv.older: Apollo 15's battery-powered rover covered 27.8 km in about three hours of driving, letting the crew reach far more geology sites than earlier missions on foot.
lrv.learned: Driving let astronauts sample many different places, which helped scientists read the Moon's history.
lrv.now: Parked on the Moon where the crew left it, its batteries long dead.

pioneer10.name: Pioneer 10
pioneer10.young: Pioneer 10 was the first probe to fly past Jupiter. It carries a metal picture message, in case anyone ever finds it.
pioneer10.older: Designed for 21 months, Pioneer 10 kept working for more than 30 years. It crossed the asteroid belt, flew past Jupiter, and carries a plaque showing where and when it came from.
pioneer10.learned: The asteroid belt could be crossed safely, and we got the first close look at Jupiter and its intense radiation.
pioneer10.now: Silent since January 2003, when its power ran too low to send a signal. It keeps coasting outward.

voyager2.name: Voyager 2
voyager2.young: The only spacecraft that has visited Uranus and Neptune. It left our Sun's bubble in 2018 and is still sending messages.
voyager2.older: Voyager 2 used a rare planetary alignment, swinging past Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. It entered interstellar space in 2018 and three of its science instruments were still running in 2026.
voyager2.learned: Our only close-up views of Uranus and Neptune, plus direct measurements of the boundary of the Sun's influence.
voyager2.now: Still working, but losing about 4 watts of power a year. In 2026 engineers swapped in lower-power devices to keep its science going.

viking1.name: Viking 1 Lander
viking1.young: The first US spacecraft to land safely on Mars. It took the first pictures from the ground and tested the soil for signs of life.
viking1.older: Viking 1 landed on 20 July 1976 and worked for more than six years. Its biology experiments found unexpected chemical activity in the soil, but no clear evidence of living things.
viking1.learned: Mars has iron-rich soil with a strongly reactive chemistry. The puzzling results shaped how we search for life today.
viking1.now: Silent since November 1982. Controllers tried for months to reach it again.

sojourner.name: Sojourner
sojourner.young: The first rover ever on Mars. It was about the size of a microwave oven and was meant to last just one week.
sojourner.older: Sojourner rolled off the Pathfinder lander in July 1997 and became the first wheeled vehicle on another planet. Planned for about seven days, it worked for 83.
sojourner.learned: Small, low-cost rovers really worked on Mars, opening the way for every rover since.
sojourner.now: Silent since 27 September 1997, when contact with its lander ended. It rests near the lander.

opportunity.name: Opportunity
opportunity.young: Built to last 90 Martian days, Opportunity kept going for almost 15 years and drove farther than a marathon!
opportunity.older: Designed for about 90 sols, Opportunity worked from 2004 to 2018 and drove over 45 km. A planet-wide dust storm blocked the sunlight its solar panels needed.
opportunity.learned: It found hematite, a mineral that usually forms with water, showing that this part of Mars was once wet.
opportunity.now: Silent since 10 June 2018. Its off-world driving record stood until Perseverance passed it in October 2026.

curiosity.name: Curiosity
curiosity.young: A rover as big as a car with a laser and a drill. It has been climbing a mountain on Mars for years.
curiosity.older: Nuclear-powered Curiosity has driven more than 38 km since 2012. In August 2026 it reached a climb of one kilometer up Mount Sharp, reading layers of rock like pages in a history book.
curiosity.learned: Ancient Gale Crater held conditions that could have supported tiny life long ago.
curiosity.now: Still driving and still doing science.

perseverance.name: Perseverance
perseverance.young: This rover is searching for signs of ancient life and packing rock samples in tubes. It is now the farthest-driving vehicle on another world!
perseverance.older: Exploring an ancient river delta and crater rim since 2021, Perseverance collects sealed rock samples. On 11 October 2026 it passed Opportunity's distance record at 45.22 km.
perseverance.learned: Jezero was once a lake fed by a river, one of the best places on Mars to look for signs of past life.
perseverance.now: Working on an extended mission planned to run through about 2028.

ingenuity.name: Ingenuity
ingenuity.young: A tiny helicopter that hitched a ride on Perseverance. It was supposed to fly 5 times. It flew 72 times!
ingenuity.older: Ingenuity was a technology test planned for up to five flights over 30 days. Instead, the first aircraft on another world flew 72 times in almost three years, until its rotor blades broke in January 2024.
ingenuity.learned: Powered flight works in Mars's thin air, opening the door to future aircraft on other worlds.
ingenuity.now: Grounded for good. NASA studied its final flight in the first aircraft accident investigation on another world.

voyager1.name: Voyager 1
voyager1.young: The farthest human-made object ever. It carries a Golden Record of sounds and pictures from Earth.
voyager1.older: After flying past Jupiter and Saturn, Voyager 1 became the first spacecraft in interstellar space in 2012. NASA says it reaches one light-day from Earth on 18 November 2026.
voyager1.learned: Discovered active volcanoes on Jupiter's moon Io and measured the space between the stars for the very first time.
voyager1.now: Still talking to us, with two science instruments left running after NASA shut one off in April 2026 to save power.

new_horizons.name: New Horizons
new_horizons.young: The first spacecraft to visit Pluto. It found a giant heart-shaped plain of ice!
new_horizons.older: New Horizons flew past Pluto in 2015 and the distant object Arrokoth in 2019. In June 2026 it woke up healthy from its longest hibernation, about 9.5 billion km from Earth.
new_horizons.learned: Pluto is a surprisingly active world with mountains of ice and glaciers of frozen nitrogen.
new_horizons.now: Still working and heading out through the Kuiper Belt. This photo is Pluto, as New Horizons saw it.

apollo12_descent.name: Apollo 12 Descent Stage
apollo12_descent.young: The lower half of Intrepid carried the astronauts to the Moon. They left it behind when they flew home.
apollo12_descent.older: Apollo 12 landed near Surveyor 3. Its descent stage stayed on the Moon while the ascent stage lifted the crew back to orbit.
apollo12_descent.learned: The crew visited a robotic spacecraft and returned pieces of it to Earth, showing how long hardware can endure on the lunar surface.
apollo12_descent.now: Still at the Apollo 12 landing site. The ascent stage, identified by the C designation, was deliberately sent into the Moon.

apollo15_descent.name: Apollo 15 Descent Stage
apollo15_descent.young: Falcon's lower stage stayed on the Moon after the astronauts launched home.
apollo15_descent.older: Apollo 15's descent stage remained at Hadley-Apennine. NASA's mission record labels the ascent stage 1971-063C and the descent stage 1971-063E.
apollo15_descent.learned: The landing site let astronauts explore mountains and a winding channel with the first lunar rover.
apollo15_descent.now: Still on the Moon beside the tracks of Apollo 15's rover.

lrv16.name: Apollo 16 Lunar Rover
lrv16.young: This moon buggy carried astronauts John Young and Charlie Duke across the lunar hills.
lrv16.older: Apollo 16's Lunar Roving Vehicle let the crew travel farther from the Orion lander to study the Descartes Highlands.
lrv16.learned: A lightweight electric rover let astronauts collect many more rock samples than they could reach on foot.
lrv16.now: Parked on the Moon near the Apollo 16 landing site.

lrv17.name: Apollo 17 Lunar Rover
lrv17.young: The last Apollo moon buggy carried astronauts across a valley of mountains and orange soil.
lrv17.older: Apollo 17's Lunar Roving Vehicle travelled 30.5 kilometers during the final crewed lunar landing mission.
lrv17.learned: The rover helped the crew collect samples from widely separated geological sites.
lrv17.now: Left at Taurus-Littrow when the crew departed the Moon.

alsep12.name: Apollo 12 ALSEP
alsep12.young: A team of instruments stayed behind to listen for moonquakes and measure the Moon after the astronauts left.
alsep12.older: Apollo 12's Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package included instruments such as a seismometer and solar-wind detector. It sent data until NASA switched off the network in 1977.
alsep12.learned: Experiments left on the surface kept doing science long after the crew returned home.
alsep12.now: The instruments are still at the Apollo 12 site, silent and exposed to lunar dust and temperature swings.

pathfinder.name: Mars Pathfinder Lander
pathfinder.young: Pathfinder used airbags to bounce safely onto Mars and delivered Sojourner, the first rover there.
pathfinder.older: The 1997 Pathfinder mission demonstrated an airbag landing system and operated from Ares Vallis for nearly three months.
pathfinder.learned: A lower-cost lander could deliver a working rover to Mars and return useful surface science.
pathfinder.now: Silent at Ares Vallis since September 27, 1997. Sojourner rests nearby.

spirit.name: Spirit
spirit.young: Spirit was Opportunity's twin. It kept exploring Mars for years after its planned 90 days.
spirit.older: Spirit landed in Gusev Crater in January 2004 and continued operating until communication ended in March 2010.
spirit.learned: Spirit found evidence that water had changed rocks at several points in Mars's past.
spirit.now: Parked in the Columbia Hills, where it became stuck in soft soil.

viking2.name: Viking 2 Lander
viking2.young: Viking 2 landed near Mars's north polar region and sent pictures and weather readings back to Earth.
viking2.older: Viking 2 touched down on September 3, 1976. Its lander operated until April 1980, while its orbiter had already stopped in 1978.
viking2.learned: Two landers and two orbiters gave scientists the first long-running view of Mars from the ground and from above.

phoenix.name: Phoenix Lander
phoenix.young: Phoenix dug into the Martian soil near the north pole and found water ice just beneath the surface.
phoenix.older: Phoenix landed in May 2008 and used a robotic arm to scoop icy soil into its onboard instruments. Contact ended as winter darkness arrived.
phoenix.learned: Water ice lies close to the surface in Mars's far north, where future explorers may need to learn how to use local resources.
phoenix.now: Silent at its northern landing site after its solar power faded in the Martian winter.

insight.name: InSight Lander
insight.young: InSight listened for marsquakes and measured heat coming from inside the planet.
insight.older: InSight placed a seismometer on the surface and recorded more than 1,300 marsquakes before dust covered its solar panels.
insight.learned: Quakes and heat flow revealed details about Mars's crust, mantle, and core.
insight.now: The mission ended in December 2022 after the lander could no longer generate enough power to communicate.

dawn.name: Dawn
dawn.young: Dawn visited two worlds in the asteroid belt: Vesta and the dwarf planet Ceres.
dawn.older: Dawn used ion propulsion to orbit Vesta and then Ceres. It ran out of hydrazine in October 2018 and could no longer point its antenna toward Earth.
dawn.learned: One spacecraft could orbit two distant worlds and compare their very different histories.
dawn.now: An inert spacecraft in a planned, long-lived orbit around Ceres.

near_shoemaker.name: NEAR Shoemaker
near_shoemaker.young: NEAR became the first spacecraft to orbit an asteroid. Then it gently landed there, even though it was not built to land.
near_shoemaker.older: After mapping asteroid Eros from orbit, NEAR Shoemaker touched down on February 12, 2001, and continued sending data for about two weeks.
near_shoemaker.learned: A careful descent gave scientists close-up images and measurements from an asteroid's surface.
near_shoemaker.now: Resting on Eros, silent since February 28, 2001.

pioneer11.name: Pioneer 11
pioneer11.young: Pioneer 11 flew past Jupiter, then used its gravity to reach Saturn. It was the first spacecraft to visit Saturn.
pioneer11.older: Launched in 1973, Pioneer 11 used a Jupiter gravity assist to reach Saturn in 1979. NASA received its last transmission in 1995.
pioneer11.learned: A planet's gravity can redirect a spacecraft without the craft firing its engine during the flyby.
pioneer11.now: Coasting out of the solar system on a trajectory toward the constellation Aquila.

kepler.name: Kepler Space Telescope
kepler.young: Kepler watched thousands of stars for tiny dips in their light that could reveal planets passing in front.
kepler.older: After its main mission and the K2 extension, Kepler ran out of fuel and was retired on October 30, 2018.
kepler.learned: Repeated, tiny changes in starlight revealed that planets are common throughout our galaxy.
kepler.now: Drifting in its safe orbit around the Sun, far behind Earth.
